label: Reconstruction from Two Views
notes: Open by framing the central question of printed pages 262 to 278: given only matching points in two uncalibrated images, which cameras and which scene points can we recover, and which residual ambiguity is unavoidable. Stress that everything in this chapter flows from that single tension between what images measure and what we want.

label: The Reconstruction Pipeline
notes: Walk the class through the four-stage loop the notebook builds: estimate the fundamental matrix from correspondences, retrieve a compatible camera pair, triangulate structure, then study the freedom that remains. Emphasize that no calibration is assumed yet, so the output is a projective reconstruction rather than a Euclidean one.

label: Retrieving Cameras from F
notes: Explain the canonical choice that breaks the gauge freedom: fix the first camera as identity, then read the second directly off the fundamental matrix using the epipole. Point out that this is one particular projective frame among infinitely many, chosen for convenience, not the true rig that produced the photographs.

label: Triangulation of a 3D Point
notes: Describe triangulation as intersecting two back-projected rays that share an epipolar plane. Build the four-row homogeneous system from the two projection equations and solve by its smallest singular vector. Note that away from the baseline the rays meet in exactly one point, giving a rank-three measurement matrix.

label: The Baseline Exception
notes: Highlight the single failure mode of triangulation. A world point lying on the baseline projects to the two epipoles, so both rays collapse onto the baseline itself and lose a rank. Connect this degeneracy to the notebook check where the measurement matrix drops from rank three to rank two.

label: The Projective Ambiguity
notes: State the reconstruction theorem precisely. Replacing every point by H times the point, and every camera by the camera times H inverse, leaves all image measurements untouched. Therefore two views fix the scene only up to a four-by-four projective transformation, and angles or parallelism in the recovered cloud are meaningless.

label: Reprojection Invariance
notes: Use the overlay to make the ambiguity concrete. The canonical reconstruction reprojects onto the measured points with essentially zero residual even though its 3D coordinates are strange. The lesson: image consistency cannot distinguish the true scene from any projective warp of it, which is why extra information is required.

label: The Stratified Ladder
notes: Introduce the three strata as a ladder of increasing structure. Projective knows only incidence, affine adds parallelism, metric adds angles and length ratios. Each rung is unlocked by identifying one geometric object: the plane at infinity for affine, the absolute conic for metric. The Euclidean scene differs only by an overall similarity.

label: Affine Upgrade
notes: Explain that the affine upgrade is exactly the act of locating the plane at infinity in the projective frame. Once that plane is moved back to its canonical position by the block homography, parallel scene directions become parallel again. The SymPy identity confirms the upgrade formula maps the chosen plane to zero zero zero one exactly.

label: Metric Upgrade via the IAC
notes: Describe the metric upgrade through the image of the absolute conic, computed from the calibration K. A Cholesky factor of the rectifying shape matrix supplies the final transform, after which right angles and length ratios are restored. Mention the calibrated route through the essential matrix and the four-fold pose decomposition resolved by cheirality.

label: Direct Upgrade from Ground Control
notes: Contrast the stratified route with the direct one. Five non-coplanar control points with known world coordinates fix the missing four-by-four homography outright, since each correspondence gives three equations. Held-out points then certify the fit. This is the practical shortcut when survey data or a known calibration object is available.

label: Synthesis and Outlook
notes: Close by consolidating the chapter into its core claims and pointing forward. Two views give projective structure for free; affine and metric structure each cost one identified geometric object. Real images add noise, motivating the robust estimation and bundle adjustment of later chapters. Leave students with the ladder image firmly in mind.
